title: Customers Who Never Ordered
description: Find the rows with no match in another table: an anti-join.
statement: Return the `name` of every customer who has **never placed an order** (of any status), in alphabetical order.
variants: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (52, 'Aaron Zero', NULL, 'US', '2025-01-01')
hints: You want the customers for whom a search in `orders` finds nothing.
Either `LEFT JOIN orders` and keep the rows where the order side is `NULL`, or `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE ...)`.
The other data gives one of these customers a cancelled order. A cancelled order is still an order.
solution:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
ORDER BY c.name;
explanation:
**The idea.** "Rows with no match" is called an **anti-join**. Two correct forms: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id)`, or a `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL`. Both say: look for a matching order, and keep the customer when there is none.

**Why not `NOT IN`.** `id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` looks the same, but if the subquery returns even one `NULL`, `NOT IN` returns *no rows at all* (a comparison with `NULL` is never true). `NOT EXISTS` has no such trap, which is why it is the safer habit.

**Usual mistakes.** `JOIN` instead of an anti-join; `<>` against a joined table (that finds customers who have *some other* order); `NOT IN` on a nullable column.
